solution:
**Given:** \(\rho = 22.4\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\), fcc so \(n = 4\), \(M = 192.2\ \mathrm{g/mol}\), \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).

**Step 1 — find the edge length from the density relation** (§1.5.2):

\(\rho = \dfrac{nM}{a^3 N_A} \quad \Rightarrow \quad a^3 = \dfrac{nM}{\rho N_A}\)

\(a^3 = \dfrac{4 \times 192.2\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{22.4\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}} = 5.699 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

\(a = (5.699 \times 10^{-23})^{1/3} = 3.848 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm} = 384.8\ \mathrm{pm}\)

**Step 2 — radius from the fcc relation** (Table 1.3), \(r = 0.3535\,a\):

\(r = 0.3535 \times 384.8\ \mathrm{pm} = 136.0\ \mathrm{pm}\)

**The radius of the iridium atom is about \(136\ \mathrm{pm}\)** (\(1.36 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\)).

**Given:** ccp (= fcc) structure, \(a = 353.6\ \mathrm{pm} = 3.536 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\).

**Part 1 — radius of the Al atom.** For an fcc/ccp lattice \(4r = \sqrt{2}\,a\), so \(r = 0.3535\,a\) (Table 1.3):

\(r = 0.3535 \times 353.6\ \mathrm{pm} = 125.0\ \mathrm{pm}\)

**Part 2 — number of unit cells in \(1.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}\).** The volume of one unit cell is \(a^3\), so

\(a^3 = (3.536 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3 = 4.421 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

Number of unit cells in volume \(V\) of metal \(= \dfrac{V}{a^3}\) (§1.7.4):

\(= \dfrac{1.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}}{4.421 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}} = 2.262 \times 10^{22}\)

**The radius of the Al atom is \(125\ \mathrm{pm}\), and \(1.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of Al contains about \(2.26 \times 10^{22}\) unit cells.**

The Y atoms form an hcp lattice. By the *Remember* box of §1.6.3, the number of tetrahedral voids is twice the number of atoms, so

number of tetrahedral voids \(= 2\mathrm{Y}\)

The X atoms occupy one third of these:

number of X atoms \(= \dfrac{1}{3} \times 2\mathrm{Y} = \dfrac{2}{3}\mathrm{Y}\)

Hence

\(\mathrm{X} : \mathrm{Y} = \dfrac{2}{3} : 1 = 2 : 3\)

**Formula of the compound \(= \mathrm{X_2Y_3}\).**

(This is the same reasoning as worked example 1.4, where the atoms filling one third of the tetrahedral voids gave \(\mathrm{A_2B_3}\).)

Both voids arise when a second hexagonal close-packed layer is laid on the first (§1.6.1 c ii). In a hexagonal close-packed layer the free spaces between the spheres are **triangular**, and the apices of the triangular voids in alternate rows point alternately upwards and downwards. The spheres of the second layer rest in the depressions of the first, but they cannot cover every triangular void.

**Tetrahedral void.** Where a triangular void of the first layer **is** covered by a sphere of the second layer, a tetrahedral void is generated. It is surrounded by four spheres — the three of the first layer plus the one resting on them — and joining the centres of those four spheres gives a tetrahedron enclosing the void (Fig. 1.6).

**Octahedral void.** The remaining triangular voids of the first layer have, directly above them, triangular voids of the second layer pointing the opposite way. These two overlapping triangular voids together form an octahedral void, which is surrounded by six spheres — three from each layer (Fig. 1.7).

In short: a depression in which a sphere of the next layer rests becomes a tetrahedral void; a depression in which no sphere rests, overlapping a depression of the layer above, becomes an octahedral void. For N particles there are 2N tetrahedral voids and N octahedral voids.

The first two layers are the same in both cases: the spheres of layer B sit in the depressions of layer A. The difference lies entirely in **where the third layer is placed** (§1.6.1 c iii).

**To form hcp:** the spheres of the third layer are placed so that they are **aligned with the spheres of the first layer** — that is, they sit over the tetrahedral voids, directly above the A spheres. The third layer is therefore itself an 'A' layer and the stacking pattern is **ABAB…** This gives the hexagonal close packed (hcp) structure; Mg and Zn crystallize this way.

**To form ccp:** the spheres of the third layer are placed so that they **cover the octahedral voids**. They then align with neither the second nor the first layer, so the third layer is a new, third kind of layer, called 'C'. Only the fourth layer aligns with the first, so the stacking pattern is **ABCABC…** This gives the cubic close packed (ccp) structure, which is the same as the fcc structure; Cu and Ag crystallize this way.

Both arrangements have coordination number 12 and packing efficiency 74 %; they differ only in this stacking sequence. Note that the question's phrase "these hexagonal close-packed structures" refers to the fact that both are built by stacking hexagonal close packed **layers** — only the ABAB… one is itself called hexagonal close packed.

The nature of a cubic unit cell is fixed by \(n\), the number of particles it contains (1 for simple cubic, 2 for bcc, 4 for fcc/ccp). Rearrange the density relation of §1.5.2 to find \(n\):

\(\rho = \dfrac{nM}{a^3 N_A} \quad \Rightarrow \quad n = \dfrac{\rho\, a^3 N_A}{M}\)

**Given:** \(M = 27\ \mathrm{g/mol}\), \(a = 405\ \mathrm{pm} = 4.05 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(\rho = 2.7\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\).

\(a^3 = (4.05 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3 = 6.643 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

\(n = \dfrac{2.7\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}} \times 6.643 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}}{27\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 4.0\)

Four particles per unit cell means the cell has particles at its eight corners and at the centres of its six faces.

**The unit cell is face-centred cubic (fcc), that is, cubic close packed (ccp).**

[Textbook misprint: the question omits the density of the element, without which it cannot be solved — both formulas needed, \(\text{unit cells} = x/(\rho a^3)\) and \(\text{atoms} = xn/(\rho a^3)\), require \(\rho\), and the stem supplies only the edge length and the mass. The book's own printed answers \(1.16 \times 10^{24}\) and \(2.32 \times 10^{24}\) are reproduced exactly by \(\rho = 7.2\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\): back-solving from the printed answer gives \(\rho = 200/(1.16 \times 10^{24} \times (2.88 \times 10^{-8})^3) = 7.22\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\), and the implied molar mass \(200 \times N_A/(2.32 \times 10^{24}) = 51.9\ \mathrm{g/mol}\) is that of chromium, which is indeed bcc. The missing datum is therefore "the density of the element is \(7.2\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\)", and it is restored in the solution below. The book's printed answers are correct once it is supplied.]

The question as printed gives only the edge length and the mass; the density is needed as well and is missing from the stem (see the bracketed note above). Taking the density as \(7.2\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\), which is the value that reproduces the book's own printed answers:

**Given:** bcc so \(n = 2\), \(a = 288\ \mathrm{pm} = 2.88 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(x = 200\ \mathrm{g}\), \(\rho = 7.2\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\).

\(a^3 = (2.88 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3 = 2.389 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

**Number of unit cells in \(x\) g** \(= \dfrac{x}{\rho a^3}\) (§1.7.4):

\(= \dfrac{200\ \mathrm{g}}{7.2\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}} \times 2.389 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}} = 1.16 \times 10^{24}\ \text{unit cells}\)

**Number of atoms in \(x\) g** \(= \dfrac{xn}{\rho a^3} = n \times (\text{number of unit cells})\), and a bcc cell holds 2 atoms:

\(= 2 \times 1.16 \times 10^{24} = 2.32 \times 10^{24}\ \text{atoms}\)

**So 200 g of the element contains about \(1.16 \times 10^{24}\) unit cells and \(2.32 \times 10^{24}\) atoms.**

All three are distinguished by the relative positions of the filled valence band and the empty conduction band — that is, by the size of the band gap (§1.9.2-1.9.4). The accompanying diagram shows the three cases (Figs. 1.23, 1.24 and 1.25 of the chapter).

**Metal conductor.** There is **no band gap**. The outermost electrons of all the atoms occupy the conduction band, which is either only partially filled (the 3s band of sodium) or overlaps a vacant band (the filled 3s and vacant 3p bands of magnesium). A large number of electrons is therefore free to move, and metals conduct well. Their conductivity **decreases** as temperature rises, because the increased vibration of the metal cations interrupts the flow of electrons. Conductivity range \(10^{4}\) to \(10^{7}\ \mathrm{ohm^{-1}\,m^{-1}}\).

**Insulator.** The valence band is completely filled and the conduction band is empty, and the two are separated by a **large** energy gap called the forbidden zone. Thermal energy is insufficient to promote electrons across it, so the conduction band stays vacant and no current flows. Conductivity range \(10^{-20}\) to \(10^{-10}\ \mathrm{ohm^{-1}\,m^{-1}}\); example, diamond, whose band gap is \(5.47\ \mathrm{eV}\).

**Semiconductor.** Like an insulator the valence band is full and the conduction band empty, but the gap between them is **small**. Above absolute zero a few electrons are thermally promoted across it, so the conduction band becomes partially filled and the valence band partially empty and the solid conducts a little. Its conductivity **increases** with temperature. Conductivity range \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{4}\ \mathrm{ohm^{-1}\,m^{-1}}\); examples, Si (\(1.12\ \mathrm{eV}\)) and Ge (\(0.67\ \mathrm{eV}\)).

**What an n-type semiconductor is.** It is an extrinsic semiconductor that contains an increased number of electrons in the conduction band. It is obtained by doping an intrinsic semiconductor of group 14 (Si or Ge) with a **group 15** element such as P, As, Sb or Bi (§1.9.5 i). Because the charge carriers are the extra **negative** electrons, the material is called n-type.

**Why its conductivity is higher than that of the pure semiconductor.** Take Si doped with phosphorus, shown in the accompanying diagram (Fig. 1.26). Each Si atom is linked tetrahedrally to four other Si atoms. When a little phosphorus is added, P atoms occupy some of the regular lattice sites in place of Si atoms, and the overall crystal structure of Si is unchanged. Phosphorus has **five** valence electrons; four of them are used in bonding to the four neighbouring Si atoms, so **one electron per P atom is left over**, surplus to bonding. That extra electron goes into the conduction band.

Doped Si therefore has many more electrons in its conduction band than pure Si, in which the only conduction electrons are the few thermally promoted across the band gap. Since it is the electrons in the conduction band that move under an applied potential and carry the current, the doped n-type material conducts far better than the pure semiconductor.

(Note that the material remains electrically neutral: each added P atom brings one extra electron and one extra proton.)

**What it is.** Frenkel defect is a stoichiometric point defect that arises when an ion of an ionic compound is **missing from its regular lattice site and occupies an interstitial position** between lattice points, as shown in the accompanying diagram (Fig. 1.16). Since the cations are usually smaller than the anions, it is more commonly the cation that moves into the interstitial space. The displaced ion leaves a vacancy at its original site and creates an interstitial defect at its new site, so a Frenkel defect can be regarded as a **combination of a vacancy defect and an interstitial defect** in the same crystal.

**Conditions for its formation** (§1.8.1 iv):
- The ionic compound must have a **large difference between the sizes of its cation and anion** (so that the small cation can fit into an interstitial space).
- The ions must have a **low coordination number**.

(For the same reason the chapter notes that Frenkel defect is not found in pure alkali metal halides — their cations are too large to occupy an interstitial space.)

**Effect on density.** **None** — the density is unchanged. No ion has left the crystal, so neither its mass nor its volume changes. (Contrast the Schottky defect, in which ions are genuinely lost and the density decreases.)

**Effect on electrical neutrality.** **None** — the crystal as a whole remains electrically neutral, because equal numbers of cations and anions are still present; only the position of one ion has changed.

This defect is found in ionic crystals such as ZnS, AgCl, AgBr, AgI and \(\mathrm{CaF_2}\).

**What it is.** An impurity defect arises when **foreign atoms — atoms different from the host atoms — are present in the crystal lattice** (§1.8.1 b).

**Its types.** There are two kinds:

1. **Substitutional impurity defect** — the foreign atoms sit at the lattice sites themselves, in place of host atoms, displacing the regular atoms from their sites. Example: brass, an alloy of Cu and Zn, in which impurity Zn atoms occupy regular sites of the host Cu atoms.
2. **Interstitial impurity defect** — the impurity atoms occupy the interstitial spaces of the lattice instead of lattice sites. Example: steel, in which Fe atoms occupy the normal lattice sites and the carbon atoms are present in the interstitial spaces.

**Formation of vacancies through aliovalent impurity.** An aliovalent ion is one whose oxidation state differs from that of the host ion. Adding such an impurity to an ionic solid creates vacancies.

The chapter's example: suppose a small amount of \(\mathrm{SrCl_2}\) is added to NaCl during its crystallization. The added \(\mathrm{Sr^{2\oplus}}\) ions (O.S. \(+2\)) occupy some of the regular sites of the host \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) ions (O.S. \(+1\)). To maintain electrical neutrality, every \(\mathrm{Sr^{2\oplus}}\) ion must remove **two** \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) ions. One of the two vacant sites so created is occupied by the \(\mathrm{Sr^{2\oplus}}\) ion itself; **the other site remains vacant**. So each aliovalent \(\mathrm{Sr^{2\oplus}}\) ion introduced leaves behind one cation vacancy in the lattice.
